inventory.label: Keystone Predator Removal
inventory.definition: Removing a predator that limits a dominant competitor can allow that competitor to displace other primary space holders.
inventory.motionThesis: Matched rocky-shore patches diverge after one sea star is removed, allowing mussels to cover other sessile organisms in the removal patch.
inventory.distinction: A sea-star and mussel primary-space example, not a claim that all predators are keystones or that community-wide diversity necessarily declines.

inventory.label: Ecological Succession
inventory.definition: Community composition changes as organisms colonize and modify a site over time.
inventory.motionThesis: Pioneer growth on exposed substrate contributes to soil development before grasses, shrubs, and woody plants establish and change in dominance.
inventory.distinction: One illustrative primary-succession trajectory rather than a universal fixed sequence or guaranteed permanent climax.

inventory.label: Metapopulation Recolonization
inventory.definition: Dispersal from occupied habitat patches can re-establish a local population after its extinction.
inventory.motionThesis: One suitable patch loses its resident, remains empty, and then receives a migrant whose reproduction restores occupancy while other patches persist.
inventory.distinction: Local extinction and recolonization rather than resurrection, global extinction, or automatic recolonization of every patch.

inventory.label: Heterogeneous Hydrogenation
inventory.definition: A solid catalyst surface promotes hydrogen addition across an unsaturated bond while the saturated product subsequently desorbs.
inventory.motionThesis: Adsorbed hydrogen separates, ethene binds nearby, two new carbon-hydrogen bonds form as the double bond becomes single, and ethane leaves the unchanged surface.
inventory.distinction: Adsorption, reaction, and desorption on a reusable solid catalyst; a schematic sequence rather than a resolved atomistic trajectory.

inventory.label: Competitive Enzyme Inhibition
inventory.definition: Competitive inhibitor binding excludes substrate binding to an enzyme, reducing substrate turnover at a given substrate concentration.
inventory.motionThesis: An unchanged inhibitor occupies a pocket while substrate waits, then leaves so substrate can bind, convert, and release products.
inventory.distinction: A reversible same-pocket example; competitive inhibition more generally means mutually exclusive binding and need not involve exactly the same physical site.

inventory.label: Micelle Self-Assembly
inventory.definition: Amphiphilic molecules can form dynamic aggregates with hydrophobic interiors and hydrophilic surfaces in water.
inventory.motionThesis: Intact head-and-tail molecules assemble with tails inward, then exchange a monomer while retaining a micellar aggregate.
inventory.distinction: A single-layer aqueous micelle rather than a bilayer vesicle or covalent polymer, with no universal aggregation number or critical concentration asserted.

inventory.label: Liquid-Liquid Extraction
inventory.definition: A solute distributes between two immiscible liquid phases, allowing transfer into a selected extraction phase.
inventory.motionThesis: Mixing expands liquid contact, four of six persistent solute tokens transfer to the upper phase, and settling restores two separated layers.
inventory.distinction: Solute partition rather than sedimentation or chemical destruction; the organic layer is not universally upper and extraction need not be complete.

inventory.label: Ion-Exchange Softening
inventory.definition: A cation-exchange resin removes dissolved hardness ions by exchanging its counterions, commonly sodium, for calcium or magnesium.
inventory.motionThesis: One divalent calcium ion replaces two sodium counterions at fixed negative sites, then a brine step restores the sodium form and removes calcium.
inventory.distinction: Charge-balanced exchange and regeneration rather than sieving, complete deionization, or calcium becoming sodium; bulk solvent and counter-anions are omitted.

inventory.label: Adsorption Breakthrough
inventory.definition: As adsorption capacity is progressively used along a fixed bed, contaminant begins appearing in its effluent.
inventory.motionThesis: Inlet molecules bind progressively farther down a bed, and later molecules escape before the last illustrated site fills.
inventory.distinction: Finite surface uptake rather than sieving; significant breakthrough can precede complete saturation.

inventory.label: Buffer Action
inventory.definition: A weak conjugate acid-base pair consumes modest added acid or base, limiting the resulting pH change.
inventory.motionThesis: Hydronium protonates a conjugate-base unit, then hydroxide removes a proton from a weak-acid unit, forming water in both challenges.
inventory.distinction: Finite chemical buffering rather than perfect pH constancy or unlimited acid absorption; bulk solvent and spectator ions are omitted.

inventory.label: SN2 Inversion
inventory.definition: A concerted backside substitution replaces a leaving group while inverting the tetrahedral arrangement at the reacting carbon.
inventory.motionThesis: A nucleophile approaches opposite a departing group while three identity-preserving substituents sweep through a planar transition geometry into the inverted arrangement.
inventory.distinction: One concerted event with no carbocation intermediate; inversion need not change an R descriptor into S.

inventory.label: Fischer Esterification
inventory.definition: Acid-catalyzed reaction of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol forms an ester and water through reversible addition and elimination steps.
inventory.motionThesis: Protonation enables alcohol addition, proton transfer creates a water leaving group, and carbonyl re-formation precedes release of the acid catalyst.
inventory.distinction: The alcohol oxygen remains in the ester and the acid hydroxyl oxygen leaves in water in this forward sequence; solvent proton shuttles are omitted.

inventory.label: Chain-Growth Polymerization
inventory.definition: Successive monomers add at a reactive chain center, transferring that center to the newly extended chain.
inventory.motionThesis: An initiating radical captures three intact carbon pairs as their double bonds become single, leaving a growing zigzag chain with the radical at its new end.
inventory.distinction: A radical example rather than all chain-growth mechanisms; hydrogens are implicit, incorporated atoms persist, and termination is not shown.

inventory.label: Elastomer Crosslinking
inventory.definition: Sparse links between flexible polymer chains form a network that limits chain sliding and supports recovery after deformation.
inventory.motionThesis: Crosslinks join separate chains, and the connected network extends and recoils by changing strand conformation while every link remains attached.
inventory.distinction: Coarse-grained strands retain contour length, rather than chemical bonds stretching by the macroscopic strain; no universal sulfur-only mechanism is asserted.

inventory.label: Sol-Gel Network Formation
inventory.definition: Reactive precursors or sol species join into an extended network that immobilizes liquid within a gel.
inventory.motionThesis: Silanol-bearing units form oxygen bridges and release water until separate species connect into one solvent-filled network.
inventory.distinction: A silica condensation stage after hydrolysis, with solvent retained rather than instantly evaporated or converted into a dense crystal.

inventory.label: Edge Dislocation Glide
inventory.definition: An edge dislocation moves along its slip plane through local atomic rearrangements, leaving a permanent relative lattice displacement behind it.
inventory.motionThesis: Local neighbor bonds switch around an advancing extra-half-plane tip, and the defect exits at a surface that retains a one-spacing slip step.
inventory.distinction: An atom-preserving kinematic construction of conservative glide, not vacancy-mediated climb, a crack, or a measured elastic-field solution.

inventory.label: Precipitation Strengthening
inventory.definition: Fine second-phase particles increase the stress required for dislocations to move through a material.
inventory.motionThesis: An advancing dislocation meets two precipitates, remains pinned at them, and bows between them under continued shear.
inventory.distinction: A pinning and bowing example before bypass, without claiming that all precipitates are impenetrable or that larger particles always strengthen a material.

inventory.label: Curvature-Driven Grain Growth
inventory.definition: In an ideal curvature-driven model, grain boundaries migrate to reduce interfacial energy, allowing one crystal orientation to replace another.
inventory.motionThesis: A circular grain shrinks as its boundary migrates inward, while the surrounding grain occupies the swept region.
inventory.distinction: An isolated isotropic two-dimensional model with area decreasing linearly, not a universal kinetic law for real polycrystals or loss of material.

inventory.label: Solid-State Sintering
inventory.definition: Diffusional mass transport bonds solid particles through growing necks and, for densifying transport routes, reduces pore space.
inventory.motionThesis: Two contacting solid particles develop a neck while material redistribution and center approach consolidate the pair.
inventory.distinction: A densifying route below melting with conserved schematic cross-sectional area, rather than an exact three-dimensional volume model; surface diffusion alone need not densify particles.

inventory.label: Martensitic Transformation
inventory.definition: A martensitic transformation changes crystal structure through coordinated atomic displacements without long-range diffusion, producing a shape strain.
inventory.motionThesis: A planar transformation front sweeps through persistent lattice sites, leaving a differently sheared product lattice and retained shape change.
inventory.distinction: A compatible schematic displacive lattice transformation, not the exact crystallography of a specific steel or a quantitative Bain-strain model.

inventory.label: Shape-Memory Recovery
inventory.definition: A suitably processed shape-memory alloy can retain a low-temperature deformation and recover its trained shape when heating reverses its martensitic transformation.
inventory.motionThesis: A thin straight wire bends under load, stays bent after the load withdraws, and straightens only when heat arrives.
inventory.distinction: A one-way trained-alloy example within its recoverable strain range, preserving schematic neutral-axis length; cooling alone does not bend the wire again.

inventory.label: Glass Tempering
inventory.definition: Rapid surface cooling of hot glass followed by core cooling leaves compressive surface layers balanced by a tensile interior.
inventory.motionThesis: The outside cools first, the core cools later, and opposing residual stress directions remain after temperature becomes uniform.
inventory.distinction: Thermal prestressing before failure, with final surface compression appearing after core cooling; the glass remains brittle.

inventory.label: Laminated Glass Retention
inventory.definition: In laminated glass, a bonded polymer interlayer can remain continuous after glass plies fracture and retain many of their fragments.
inventory.motionThesis: Impact creates separate rigid glass pieces while a continuous flexible middle layer stretches between them and holds the fractured span.
inventory.distinction: A schematic example of fragment adhesion and polymer bridging, without implying that all fragments remain attached or that the broken panel retains its original strength.

inventory.label: Pitting Corrosion
inventory.definition: Local breakdown of a passive surface film can permit concentrated anodic metal dissolution, producing a growing cavity whose local solution chemistry sustains attack.
inventory.motionThesis: A small film opening leads to an undercut liquid-filled cavity as metal ions leave its receding wall and chloride enrichment and acidity develop inside.
inventory.distinction: A schematic stable-pit example with persistent damage, not a universal growth law; chloride remains an ion, and many film defects can repassivate.

inventory.label: Aluminum Anodizing
inventory.definition: An applied anodic potential converts surface aluminum into a thicker adherent oxide through ionic transport across the film.
inventory.motionThesis: The metal-oxide boundary recedes into aluminum while a compact oxide layer grows outward and inward under applied positive polarity.
inventory.distinction: A compact barrier-film example grown from the substrate, with schematic thickness and metal-consumption ratios; no porous or dyed coating is implied.

inventory.label: Electroplating
inventory.definition: Electric current reduces dissolved metal ions onto a conductive workpiece, building a metal coating at the cathode.
inventory.motionThesis: Copper leaves a soluble positive anode as ions and joins the negative workpiece as neutral metal, thickening its coating.
inventory.distinction: A one-sided soluble copper-anode example with equal schematic lost and deposited areas, not substrate oxidation or liquid paint application.

inventory.label: Atomic Layer Deposition
inventory.definition: Alternating, separated precursor exposures build a thin film through surface reactions that stop when available reactive sites are consumed.
inventory.motionThesis: One precursor saturates finite sites, excess vapor clears, a second precursor reacts with the bound groups, and the sequence repeats to coat a trench conformally.
inventory.distinction: Abstract precursor and functional-group symbols illustrate two separated self-limiting exposures and purges; one cycle need not form a complete crystallographic monolayer.

inventory.label: Photolithographic Pattern Transfer
inventory.definition: Patterned light changes a resist’s solubility so development creates a mask that transfers selected openings into an underlying film by etching.
inventory.motionThesis: Light reaches two apertures, exposed positive resist dissolves, the uncovered film is etched, and remaining resist strips away to reveal matching gaps.
inventory.distinction: A positive-resist process with separate exposure, development, schematic directional selective etching, and stripping; the substrate remains intact.

inventory.label: Injection Molding
inventory.definition: A measured shot of molten polymer is forced into a closed mold, cooled into a discrete part, and ejected after the mold opens.
inventory.motionThesis: A reciprocating screw advances to fill a shaped cavity, the filled part cools in place, and ejector pins release it only after the mold separates.
inventory.distinction: A hot-runner schematic with a closed gate before ejection and matched reservoir loss and cavity-plus-runner fill; the real packing and cooling stages are simplified.

inventory.label: Polymer Extrusion
inventory.definition: A rotating screw conveys and plasticizes polymer, building pressure that drives a continuous melt stream through a shaping die.
inventory.motionThesis: Pellets enter screw channels, merge into melt, and emerge through a fixed opening as a continuous profile that swells slightly and cools downstream.
inventory.distinction: A continuous side-view profile with a stationary screw axis and die, schematic swell, and approximately constant cross-sectional material flux; screw heating is not attributed solely to external heaters.

inventory.label: Extrusion Blow Molding
inventory.definition: An extruded hollow polymer tube is enclosed and pinched in a split mold, inflated against the cavity, cooled, and released as a hollow part.
inventory.motionThesis: A hanging tube seals at its base before air enters its lumen and expands its thinning walls into a bottle-shaped cavity.
inventory.distinction: A schematic thinning hollow shell with a retained pinch-off flash, not an exact volume simulation; the captured parison separates at the neck before inflation and retains its shape after venting.

inventory.label: Hot Rolling Reduction
inventory.definition: Opposing rolls plastically compress a hot solid workpiece, reducing thickness while increasing its length and exit speed.
inventory.motionThesis: A marked strip enters the roll bite thick and slow, compresses along the roll surfaces, and exits thinner with larger spacing between the same material markers.
inventory.distinction: A constant-width, approximately constant-density plane-strain schematic with material flux conserved; width spread, elastic recovery, and recrystallization kinetics are omitted.

inventory.label: Continuous Casting
inventory.definition: Molten metal continuously enters a water-cooled bottomless mold, develops a supporting solid shell, and is withdrawn while secondary cooling solidifies its core.
inventory.motionThesis: A stationary shell-and-core profile surrounds steadily descending material while mold oscillation and withdrawal rolls separate solidification from transport.
inventory.distinction: A steady illustrative thermal profile, not a universal heat-transfer law; the strand has a supporting shell before withdrawal and no cutoff is shown above core closure.

inventory.label: Laser Powder Bed Fusion
inventory.definition: A laser selectively melts successive thin powder layers so solidified tracks bond to the underlying part and build a three-dimensional object.
inventory.motionThesis: A recoater spreads powder, a scanning laser leaves a fused track, the build descends one layer, and a second narrower track creates a stepped section.
inventory.distinction: A two-layer cross-section with a moving local melt pool and unfused surrounding powder; powder, track, and platform motions are schematic rather than process-scale measurements.

inventory.label: Catalytic Cracking
inventory.definition: Hot hydrocarbons contact a catalyst and undergo carbon-carbon bond cleavage and related reactions, producing smaller hydrocarbon molecules.
inventory.motionThesis: One persistent eight-carbon backbone adsorbs at a catalyst and separates into four-carbon alkane and alkene backbones before both products depart.
inventory.distinction: An atom-balanced net C8H18 to C4H10 plus C4H8 example with one tracked hydrogen transfer and other hydrogens implicit; intermediates and alternative products are omitted rather than implying an elementary concerted scissor reaction.

inventory.label: Haber-Bosch Synthesis
inventory.definition: Industrial ammonia synthesis reacts nitrogen with hydrogen over a catalyst at elevated temperature and pressure; on iron, adsorbed reactants dissociate and nitrogen is hydrogenated before ammonia desorbs.
inventory.motionThesis: One nitrogen molecule and three hydrogen pairs dissociate on iron, then three staged additions per nitrogen yield two departing ammonia molecules with all eight atoms retained.
inventory.distinction: An iron-surface mechanism schematic with staged hydrogenation, not complete conversion per industrial pass or the entire industrial recycle plant.

inventory.label: Chlor-Alkali Membrane Cell
inventory.definition: A cation-selective membrane separates brine electrolysis compartments, yielding chlorine at the anode and hydrogen plus aqueous sodium hydroxide at the cathode.
inventory.motionThesis: Chloride pairs discharge on the positive side, water supplies hydrogen on the negative side, and sodium ions cross the divider while both gas products remain separated.
inventory.distinction: The balanced net two sodium chlorides plus two waters yield chlorine, hydrogen, and two aqueous sodium hydroxides; membrane transport is predominantly sodium ions with water, and dissolved ions are not drawn as bonded sodium hydroxide molecules.

inventory.label: Basic Oxygen Steelmaking
inventory.definition: Oxygen blown into carbon-rich molten iron oxidizes excess carbon and other constituents; carbon leaves largely in carbon-monoxide-rich off-gas while oxide products enter a basic slag, refining the melt into steel.
inventory.motionThesis: An oxygen jet meets a liquid-metal bath, and six tracked dissolved-carbon marks become rising carbon-monoxide pairs while slag remains a distinct layer and some carbon stays dissolved.
inventory.distinction: A balanced carbon-removal example within liquid-metal refining, not ore reduction, whole-bath oxidation, or a quantitative carbon-content model.

inventory.label: Froth Flotation
inventory.definition: Selectively hydrophobic mineral surfaces attach to air bubbles in a slurry and rise into a recoverable froth, while predominantly wetted gangue remains in the pulp.
inventory.motionThesis: Selected grains pin to bubble interfaces and ride into an overflowing froth, while unselected grains remain submerged or deflect around passing bubbles.
inventory.distinction: An idealized interfacial-wettability separation with persistent grains, not density-only sorting or guaranteed complete recovery; entrainment and detachment are omitted.

inventory.label: Spray Drying
inventory.definition: A liquid feed is atomized into droplets that contact hot drying gas; solvent evaporates and the retained nonvolatile material becomes collectable dry particles.
inventory.motionThesis: A liquid jet divides into descending droplets whose solvent envelopes shrink around persistent solid contents, while vapor exits with the gas and dry particles fall into a collector.
inventory.distinction: A compact-particle example of solvent removal from liquid feed, not spray congealing or a universal final-particle morphology; material glyphs and rates are schematic.

inventory.label: Freeze Drying
inventory.definition: A frozen product loses ice by sublimation under reduced pressure during primary drying, then secondary drying removes residual bound moisture and leaves a porous solid matrix.
inventory.motionThesis: A sublimation front retreats through a fixed scaffold as vapor deposits as ice on a colder condenser, followed by a smaller release of bound moisture.
inventory.distinction: The product starts already frozen and retains its solid scaffold; the depicted mechanism is not liquid boiling, matrix shrinkage, or current regulatory guidance from the historical source.

inventory.label: Gas-Solid Fluidization
inventory.definition: Upward gas flow supports and expands a bed of solid particles when drag balances their effective weight.
inventory.motionThesis: Thirty-six persistent grains expand into an individually moving bed under upward gas flow and resettle as the flow subsides.
inventory.distinction: An illustrative gas-solid bed with conserved grains and no liquid; particle paths demonstrate expansion rather than a quantitative hydrodynamic simulation.

inventory.label: Vacuum Degassing of Steel
inventory.definition: Reduced pressure promotes removal of dissolved gases from molten steel, while argon stirring renews the liquid-gas interface and assists transport.
inventory.motionThesis: Six of eight dissolved hydrogen markers collect into three hydrogen pairs inside rising argon bubbles and leave through a vacuum duct, while two remain in the melt.
inventory.distinction: A hydrogen-removal example with persistent material identities, not oxygen blowing, steel boiling, or complete elimination of dissolved gas.

inventory.label: Gestalt Proximity
inventory.definition: Nearby visual elements tend to be perceived as belonging to a group.
inventory.motionThesis: Sixteen identical dots change their relative horizontal and vertical spacing so perceived columns reorganize into rows.
inventory.distinction: Grouping by spatial distance, without color, connecting lines, or shared-motion membership cues; a perceptual tendency rather than a guaranteed response.

inventory.label: Gestalt Common Fate
inventory.definition: Visual elements moving together tend to be perceived as a group.
inventory.motionThesis: Twelve identical interleaved dots form two groups through opposite synchronized vertical motion.
inventory.distinction: Appearance stays identical while common velocity groups spatially interleaved elements; unlike proximity grouping, membership is specified by motion.

inventory.label: Amodal Completion
inventory.definition: A partly occluded object is perceived as continuing behind an occluder even though its hidden portion is not directly visible.
inventory.motionThesis: An opaque screen covers the middle of a continuous diagonal bar, slides aside to reveal its continuity, and returns.
inventory.distinction: Completion behind an actual occluding surface, without drawing or exposing a hidden segment; distinct from an illusory contour in an unoccluded region.

inventory.label: Kanizsa Illusory Contour
inventory.definition: Aligned inducing fragments can evoke an apparent contour where no physical luminance edge defines the implied sides.
inventory.motionThesis: Three cutout disks rotate into inward alignment and hold, suggesting a triangle whose sides are never drawn.
inventory.distinction: Only the actual inducers are rendered; the apparent triangle has no stroke, fill, glow, or luminance difference from the surrounding background.

inventory.label: Motion Parallax
inventory.definition: Observer translation produces depth-dependent relative image motion in a stationary scene.
inventory.motionThesis: One translating viewpoint produces progressively smaller opposite image displacements for landmarks at one, two, and four relative depths.
inventory.distinction: A fixed-orientation pinhole projection with identical stationary world landmarks, not object motion or two simultaneous binocular views; row spacing separates depth examples schematically.

inventory.label: Binocular Disparity
inventory.definition: Corresponding scene features occupy different relative positions in the two eyes’ images, providing a depth cue relative to fixation.
inventory.motionThesis: A target changing depth makes matched left and right image markers separate, coincide at a reference, and reverse their relative offsets.
inventory.distinction: A rectified pinhole diagram of relative image positions, not eyeball rotation or a claim that the two panels themselves produce stereoscopic fusion.

inventory.label: Aperture Problem
inventory.definition: A straight edge viewed through a small aperture specifies its perpendicular motion but leaves tangential motion ambiguous.
inventory.motionThesis: Two diagonal bars moving in different directions look identical through small windows until expanding apertures reveal their different endpoint trajectories.
inventory.distinction: Both local line equations remain identical while one whole bar translates horizontally and the other vertically; the windows reveal correspondence information that was initially hidden.

inventory.label: Biological Motion
inventory.definition: Coordinated motion of sparse body landmarks supports perception of an animate figure and its action.
inventory.motionThesis: Thirteen isolated lights follow articulated shoulder, elbow, wrist, hip, knee, ankle, and head positions through a coordinated walking cycle.
inventory.distinction: A stylized kinematic gait with fixed limb lengths at sampled poses, not recorded motion capture, diagnostic classification, or a rigid common-motion group.

inventory.label: Visual Pop-Out
inventory.definition: A target sufficiently different from surrounding items in a salient basic feature can be found efficiently.
inventory.motionThesis: Complete arrays appear together, each with one tilted bar among vertical bars, and target location changes only between presentations.
inventory.distinction: An orientation feature singleton without target-only flashes, color, scanning, or locator cues; efficient search is a tendency, not an instantaneous or attention-free guarantee.

inventory.label: Mental Rotation
inventory.definition: Comparison of differently oriented objects can involve mentally transforming one orientation into another.
inventory.motionThesis: A rigidly rotating pentomino aligns with a reference, followed by a mirror foil that remains different after the same in-plane rotation.
inventory.distinction: A displayed illustration of spatial comparison, not direct observation of a mental image or a reaction-time measurement; shapes do not morph during alignment.

inventory.label: Necker Cube
inventory.definition: An unchanged ambiguous wireframe cube supports competing depth interpretations.
inventory.motionThesis: The central wireframe remains identical while external annotation frames alternate between two possible front-face readings.
inventory.distinction: Only explanatory cues alternate; the ambiguous stimulus never changes, and cue timing neither measures nor prescribes a viewer’s perceptual reversals.

inventory.label: Change Blindness
inventory.definition: Observers may fail to notice a scene change when an interruption removes its localized transient cue.
inventory.motionThesis: Two nearly identical arrays alternate through whole-field blanks, then uninterrupted transitions and a delayed locator reveal one orientation change.
inventory.distinction: A temporal change demonstration with no unique target orientation or locator in the masked phase; visibility depends on viewing conditions and the observer.

inventory.label: Visual Crowding
inventory.definition: Nearby flankers can impair identification of a peripheral target that is identifiable in isolation.
inventory.motionThesis: A sharp target remains fixed relative to fixation while neighboring letters move apart, reducing crowding without changing the target’s size or contrast.
inventory.distinction: An illustrative peripheral identification task, not image blur or feature search; spacing and eccentricity are not calibrated universal thresholds.

inventory.label: Plosive Speech Release
inventory.definition: Releasing a complete oral closure can produce a brief acoustic burst as built-up air pressure escapes.
inventory.motionThesis: A side-view bilabial closure traps oral pressure, then the lips part and a brief escaping-air burst coincides with an acoustic transient.
inventory.distinction: An audibly released voiceless bilabial [p] schematic, not every stop realization, recorded speech, or a claim about aspiration duration; no nasal tract or vowel is depicted.

inventory.label: Inverted Pendulum Stabilization
inventory.definition: Horizontal cart feedback balances a freely pivoting pole near its unstable upright equilibrium.
inventory.motionThesis: A leaning pole is caught by accelerating its cart beneath it, then braking and smaller corrections restore balance.
inventory.distinction: An actively translated pivot stabilizes an unpowered upright joint; a precomputed nonlinear cart-pole response illustrates feedback rather than passive pendulum motion.

inventory.label: Ball-and-Beam Control
inventory.definition: Feedback tilts a beam so gravity accelerates and brakes a rolling ball toward a commanded position.
inventory.motionThesis: A ball rolls toward a central target, counter-tilt brakes it, and progressively smaller corrections settle it at the beam center.
inventory.distinction: Ball motion and beam slope satisfy a solid-sphere rolling approximation with small beam-motion effects neglected; the ball is not attached to the rocking beam.

inventory.label: PID Position Tracking
inventory.definition: Proportional error, accumulated error, and velocity damping combine to drive an actuator toward a commanded position.
inventory.motionThesis: A carriage follows a target step as proportional drive, integral memory, and derivative braking change with its error and motion.
inventory.distinction: An unsaturated tracking example uses derivative on measurement and an integral preload that balances a constant load; saturation handling is demonstrated separately.

inventory.label: Integrator Anti-Windup
inventory.definition: Conditional integration stops error memory from growing when a saturated actuator cannot provide the requested effort.
inventory.motionThesis: Two identical saturated loops accumulate different integral memory, so the clamped loop recovers sooner when an initially unreachable target returns within reach.
inventory.distinction: A paired comparison of conditional integration with ordinary integral action, not back-calculation, actuator hard-stop geometry, or ordinary unsaturated PID tuning.

inventory.label: Model Predictive Control
inventory.definition: A controller repeatedly optimizes a finite sequence of constrained future actions, executes the first action, and replans from the resulting state.
inventory.motionThesis: Short predicted paths extend around an obstacle; only the first segment becomes actual motion before a fresh horizon starts from the robot’s new position.
inventory.distinction: A precomputed constrained three-step discrete optimization, with unexecuted predictions discarded at each update, rather than a fixed global path or potential-field steering.

inventory.label: Differential Drive
inventory.definition: Independent coaxial wheel speeds combine into forward translation and rotation of a mobile robot.
inventory.motionThesis: Equal wheel speeds move a chassis straight, unequal speeds bend its path, and opposing speeds turn it in place.
inventory.distinction: A two-wheel no-slip kinematic example with no direct sideways translation; tread cues and signed speed arrows are synchronized with the chassis path.

inventory.label: Inverse Kinematics
inventory.definition: Inverse kinematics finds joint angles that place a robot’s end effector at a desired target.
inventory.motionThesis: Successive rigid-arm configurations shorten the tip-to-target error, and a second fixed target triggers another numerical solve.
inventory.distinction: A two-link planar Newton solve on one elbow branch, with joint-angle interpolation preserving link lengths rather than moving targets or morphing links.

inventory.label: Kinematic Singularity
inventory.definition: At a singular configuration, a robot’s Jacobian loses rank and an instantaneous end-effector motion direction becomes unavailable.
inventory.motionThesis: A bent arm straightens as its velocity ellipse collapses to a vertical line, leaving vertical tip velocity available while horizontal velocity is blocked.
inventory.distinction: An instantaneous local velocity limitation, not permanent inability to retract through subsequent finite bending, target reaching, or redundant self-motion.

inventory.label: Redundant Manipulator Null Motion
inventory.definition: A redundant manipulator changes its internal joint configuration while preserving the specified end-effector task coordinates.
inventory.motionThesis: Three rigid links reconfigure continuously while their round endpoint remains at a fixed target crosshair.
inventory.distinction: The task constrains two-dimensional tip position only; terminal orientation may change, unlike a fully constrained gripper pose.

inventory.label: Compliant Impedance Control
inventory.definition: Feedback shapes a robot’s force–displacement response so it yields predictably to contact and returns with damping.
inventory.motionThesis: An external pusher deflects a robot tip from its fixed desired position, stretching a virtual spring before the tip settles back after release.
inventory.distinction: Controlled yielding under external force, using an illustrative critically damped impedance response rather than ordinary position tracking or orthogonal hybrid motion-force control.

inventory.label: SLAM Loop Closure
inventory.definition: Recognizing a previously visited place adds a nonconsecutive pose constraint that corrects accumulated map and trajectory estimation drift.
inventory.motionThesis: An estimated route fails to close, then a matched place adds a closure edge and past pose estimates adjust together around a fixed anchor.
inventory.distinction: A simplified translation-only pose-graph optimization adjusts historical estimates, not physical robot positions, background buildings, or future planned routes.

inventory.label: Configuration-Space Obstacles
inventory.definition: Collision-producing robot configurations form forbidden regions; a translating circular robot can be replaced by its center point when obstacles expand by its radius.
inventory.motionThesis: An upper disc skirts a physical obstacle while its lower center-point counterpart follows the corresponding route around a radius-expanded obstacle.
inventory.distinction: A collision-equivalent geometry transformation, not another path planner; both obstacles and workspace boundaries account for the robot’s footprint.

inventory.label: Artificial Potential Field Navigation
inventory.definition: Attractive goal and repulsive obstacle gradients combine into a local steering command that can stall at a nonglobal minimum.
inventory.motionThesis: A robot enters a U-shaped obstacle toward a goal beyond its back wall, then stops when opposing attraction and repulsion balance.
inventory.distinction: A local steering failure at a U-shaped trap, not a feasible global path or a finite-horizon predictive optimization; numerical units and field strengths are illustrative.

inventory.label: Hybrid Motion-Force Control
inventory.definition: A robot controls motion in unconstrained directions while controlling force against contact constraints.
inventory.motionThesis: An eraser slides tangentially along a rigid surface while its normal contact force stays constant, including through sliding-direction reversal.
inventory.distinction: Independent tangential velocity and normal force act in orthogonal directions; the pad maintains exact surface contact rather than penetrating the plane or yielding under an external pusher.

inventory.label: Force-Closure Grasp
inventory.definition: A planar grasp has force closure when admissible frictional contact wrenches can oppose every planar disturbance direction, assuming sufficient actuation.
inventory.motionThesis: Two fingertips pinch a rectangle while friction-cone force vectors resist a downward load and then a turning moment without moving the object.
inventory.distinction: Planar frictional wrench capability, not unlimited load capacity, geometric enclosure alone, or full three-dimensional force closure from two hard point contacts.

inventory.label: Omnidirectional Mecanum Drive
inventory.definition: A mobile drive uses four independently driven wheels with angled passive rollers to translate in any planar direction and rotate.
inventory.motionThesis: Opposite diagonal wheel pairs reverse their rotation to slide a fixed-heading chassis sideways, then equal wheel speeds drive it forward around a closed path.
inventory.distinction: Alternating roller handedness permits direct strafing unavailable to conventional differential drive; wheel travel follows a zero-yaw kinematic mapping, with detailed traction and roller dynamics schematic.

inventory.label: Tendon-Driven Soft Gripper
inventory.definition: Offset tendons bend compliant fingers inward to grasp delicate objects.
inventory.motionThesis: A capstan reels inner tendons while continuously curved fingers close against a supported berry, hold, and elastically reopen.
inventory.distinction: An illustrative two-finger constant-curvature cross-section links cable shortening to bending; it does not reproduce the referenced three-finger prototype or its full controller.

inventory.label: Backlash Deadband
inventory.definition: Mechanical clearance lets an input reverse through a finite interval before its output moves.
inventory.motionThesis: A driving peg crosses a carriage slot after each reversal while the output pauses, then catches the opposite shoulder and drives it one to one.
inventory.distinction: A geometric play operator with memory and a twelve-unit reversal gap; the output is neither an instantaneous dead zone nor a delayed copy of the input.

inventory.label: Sampling Aliasing
inventory.definition: Insufficient temporal sampling can make distinct continuous signals produce identical sampled values.
inventory.motionThesis: Nine equally spaced samples on a seven-cycle sinusoid also lie on a one-cycle ghost curve, exposing the ambiguity of eight samples per interval.
inventory.distinction: A fixed seven-cycle signal and negative one-cycle alias agree at all nine shown sample positions; the illustration reveals reconstruction ambiguity without claiming the input changes frequency.

inventory.label: Amplitude Quantization
inventory.definition: Amplitude quantization maps a continuous input to one of a finite set of representative levels.
inventory.motionThesis: A continuously moving input crosses eight bands while the output jumps between their midpoints and a bracket shows the bounded rounding error.
inventory.distinction: Uniform midpoint quantization without overload; the deterministic amplitude error is not depicted as random noise or temporal sampling.

inventory.label: Successive-Approximation ADC
inventory.definition: A successive-approximation converter holds an input voltage and resolves its binary code by testing DAC bits from most to least significant.
inventory.motionThesis: Four weighted DAC contributions are tried in order, keeping those below a held input and clearing overshoots to retain the four-bit code 1010.
inventory.distinction: A logical four-weight DAC and ordinary input-minus-DAC comparator show four comparisons for an input of 0.68; this is not a physical capacitor-array diagram.

inventory.label: Sigma-Delta Modulation
inventory.definition: A sigma-delta modulator integrates conversion error and feeds back a coarse quantized output to produce a rapidly varying bitstream.
inventory.motionThesis: An accumulator adds each input, emits a bit at its threshold, and subtracts feedback so eight clocks at one-quarter input produce two ones while three-quarter input produces six.
inventory.distinction: A first-order unipolar accumulator example shows pulse density and residual error feedback; sixteen displayed clocks are not a complete high-resolution ADC or decimation filter.

inventory.label: Lock-In Detection
inventory.definition: Lock-in detection multiplies a measurement by a synchronized reference and averages the product to extract its coherent component.
inventory.motionThesis: A chopped optical measurement is AC-coupled and multiplied by a sign reference, making paired interference lobes cancel over a complete window while the coherent mean remains.
inventory.distinction: A deterministic two-frequency interference example uses a square-wave reference; it does not imply that arbitrary noise or the reference’s odd harmonics always cancel.

inventory.label: Phase-Locked Loop
inventory.definition: A phase-locked loop feeds oscillator timing error back to adjust its frequency toward a reference.
inventory.motionThesis: A delayed oscillator’s edges arrive progressively earlier as shrinking phase-detector correction pulses bring them close to reference edges.
inventory.distinction: An illustrative discrete timing correction reduces delay by a factor of 0.55 per comparison; it depicts active edge synchronization rather than amplitude demodulation or an exact analog filter response.

inventory.label: Quadrature Encoder
inventory.definition: Two cyclic sensor channels offset by a quarter cycle encode incremental position and direction.
inventory.motionThesis: Two patterned disk tracks produce staggered sensor transitions, and reversing rotation reverses both their order and the accumulated count.
inventory.distinction: Optical channel transduction and edge decoding are shown directly, with clockwise rotation defined as positive count; the sensor signals derive from the same moving pattern.

inventory.label: Strain-Gauge Wheatstone Bridge
inventory.definition: A Wheatstone bridge converts a strain-induced resistance change into a differential voltage.
inventory.motionThesis: A bonded foil meander lengthens and contracts, changing one bridge arm while a signed differential output crosses zero with the strain.
inventory.distinction: A quarter-bridge model uses gauge factor two and strain of plus or minus 0.002, with foil deformation exaggerated fiftyfold; tension in the upper-left arm produces a negative left-minus-right voltage.

inventory.label: LVDT Displacement Sensor
inventory.definition: An LVDT measures a movable magnetic core’s position through the difference between two transformer secondary outputs.
inventory.motionThesis: A sliding core strengthens one secondary coupling and weakens the other, making their opposed output pass through a central null and reverse phase.
inventory.distinction: An ideal balanced linear-range model shows simultaneous schematic AC waveforms and exact cancellation at center; real leakage, mismatch, and demodulator details are omitted.

inventory.label: Time-Domain Reflectometry
inventory.definition: Time-domain reflectometry locates impedance changes by measuring the delay and polarity of a reflected electrical signal.
inventory.motionThesis: Identical voltage pulses enter open-ended and shorted lines, returning with preserved and inverted polarity after the same round-trip delay.
inventory.distinction: An ideal lossless line with a matched source shows summed incident and reflected voltages, boundary doubling or cancellation, and round-trip distance inference; geometric units are illustrative.

inventory.label: Oscilloscope Triggering
inventory.definition: An oscilloscope trigger aligns waveform records to a specified signal event such as a rising threshold crossing.
inventory.motionThesis: Free-running records start at different signal phases while triggered records keep the same rising threshold crossing at a fixed pretrigger position.
inventory.distinction: Five acquisitions demonstrate a chosen time origin with twenty percent pretrigger data; the signal frequency stays constant and falling crossings do not initiate these records.

inventory.label: Sample-and-Hold
inventory.definition: A sample-and-hold circuit tracks an analog input while a switch is closed and stores its voltage on a capacitor when the switch opens.
inventory.motionThesis: The switch opens while the capacitor and output retain a captured voltage despite the continuing input waveform, then closes to resume tracking.
inventory.distinction: An ideal zero-leakage analog memory holds continuous voltages without quantization; equal input and stored voltage at reconnection avoid an unmodeled acquisition transient.

inventory.label: Pulse-Width Modulation
inventory.definition: Pulse-width modulation varies the on-time fraction of repeated fixed-period pulses to control their average value.
inventory.motionThesis: Equal-period sawtooth ramps cross successively higher thresholds, extending each output pulse’s width while its period and amplitude stay fixed.
inventory.distinction: A shared ramp-comparison model generates quarter-, half-, and three-quarter-duty pulses; this changes duration within each period rather than pulse density through error feedback.

inventory.label: Heterodyne Frequency Mixing
inventory.definition: A nonlinear mixer combines a signal and local oscillator to create components at their sum and difference frequencies.
inventory.motionThesis: Two unequal-frequency inputs meet at a multiplier, produce sum and difference components, and a filter retains the lower intermediate frequency.
inventory.distinction: Ideal multiplication of five-cycle and four-cycle cosines produces equal half-amplitude components at one and nine cycles; this is continuous frequency conversion rather than aliasing or a zero-frequency lock-in result.

inventory.label: Phased-Array Beam Steering
inventory.definition: A phased array steers its radiation pattern by controlling relative phases across stationary antenna elements.
inventory.motionThesis: Progressive feed phases change together and the computed main radiation lobe turns while all five physical antenna elements remain fixed.
inventory.distinction: The drawing shows the normalized far-field power array factor for five equally weighted half-wavelength-spaced elements, including sidelobes; it is not a near-field map or a rotating antenna.

inventory.label: Capacitive Touch Sensing
inventory.definition: A capacitive touch sensor detects the increase in electrode-to-ground capacitance produced by a nearby finger.
inventory.motionThesis: A finger approaches an insulated electrode, adds a capacitive path through the body, and makes a charge-to-threshold measurement take longer.
inventory.distinction: An illustrative self-capacitance RC readout compares normalized capacitances of seven-sixths and two; it is not mutual-capacitance sensing, a literal whole-finger plate model, or a specific commercial controller implementation.

inventory.label: MEMS Capacitive Accelerometer
inventory.definition: A MEMS accelerometer senses inertial proof-mass displacement through changes in opposing capacitances.
inventory.motionThesis: An accelerating housing moves around a spring-suspended mass, narrowing one electrode gap and widening the other to produce a signed differential signal.
inventory.distinction: Magnified steady-state motion follows an ideal damped base-excited oscillator; the phase-lagged displacement and normalized capacitance difference are not labeled as instantaneous acceleration without dynamic calibration.

inventory.label: Pumped Hydroelectric Storage
inventory.definition: Pumped hydroelectric storage uses electricity to lift water to an upper reservoir and releases electricity as the water returns through a turbine.
inventory.motionThesis: A conserved water inventory transfers between two reservoirs while pipe flow and electrical power reverse between pumping and generation.
inventory.distinction: Two equal-area reservoirs and a reversible machine show closed-inventory energy storage, with changing hydraulic head and ideal illustrative power rather than a continuously supplied hydroelectric dam.

inventory.label: Flywheel Energy Storage
inventory.definition: A motor-generator stores electrical energy as rotor kinetic energy and recovers it by decelerating the rotor.
inventory.motionThesis: A rotor spins in one direction, accelerates while electrical power enters, and slows while power flows back out through the same motor-generator.
inventory.distinction: Integrated angular motion and energy proportional to squared speed show ideal reversible storage; discharge never reverses the rotor and no real-system efficiency is claimed.

inventory.label: PEM Fuel Cell
inventory.definition: A PEM fuel cell routes hydrogen-derived protons through an ion-conducting membrane and electrons through an external load, then combines them with oxygen to form water.
inventory.motionThesis: Two hydrogen molecules yield four protons and four externally routed electrons, which join one split oxygen molecule to release two water molecules.
inventory.distinction: Separated ion and electron routes and conserved hydrogen/oxygen atoms show continuously supplied fuel conversion; the staged cycle is not an electrolysis reversal or a measured transport rate.

inventory.label: Redox Flow Battery
inventory.definition: A redox flow battery stores rechargeable energy in the oxidation states of two separately tanked, circulating electrolytes.
inventory.motionThesis: Two isolated liquid loops keep circulating at constant volume while electrical current, membrane ion compensation, and electrode redox conversion reverse.
inventory.distinction: An ideal well-mixed acidic vanadium schematic uses left V(III)/V(II) and right V(IV)/V(V) oxidation-state mixtures; bulk vanadium electrolyte never crosses the membrane and colored fractions do not represent changing liquid levels.

inventory.label: Wind-Turbine Pitch Regulation
inventory.definition: Wind-turbine pitch regulation changes blade pitch to control rotor speed or power in strong wind.
inventory.motionThesis: All three blades twist together as a gust varies, reducing their projected chord and aerodynamic torque while a feedback response bounds rotor-speed deviation.
inventory.distinction: An illustrative periodic linearized controller couples gust, pitch, and integrated rotor speed; a magnified blade section turns toward its relative wind as pitch-to-feather increases, without claiming calibrated turbine aerodynamics.

inventory.label: H-Bridge Inverter
inventory.definition: An H-bridge inverter uses four controlled switches to reverse the polarity applied from a DC source to a load.
inventory.motionThesis: Alternating diagonal switch pairs create opposite current paths through one resistor, separated by visible all-open dead intervals.
inventory.distinction: An ideal purely resistive load has zero current during dead time; the displayed bipolar output is not sinusoidal and requires no omitted inductive freewheel path.

inventory.label: Buck Converter
inventory.definition: A buck converter uses a switched inductor and freewheel diode to provide a lower DC voltage while load current continues between switch pulses.
inventory.motionThesis: Source-fed and diode-recirculation paths alternate while inductor current rises during switch-on and falls without reversing during switch-off.
inventory.distinction: An exact ideal continuous-conduction solution couples inductor current and capacitor voltage for a half-duty circuit; capacitor ripple is retained and an open switch never interrupts the positive inductor current.

inventory.label: Transformer Mutual Induction
inventory.definition: Changing magnetic flux shared by transformer windings induces terminal voltages proportional to their turn counts.
inventory.motionThesis: Four primary turns and eight secondary turns share reversing core flux while the secondary voltage stays twice the primary and both vanish at flux extrema.
inventory.distinction: Matched dotted-terminal voltage conventions and a resistive secondary load show ideal step-up transformer action; flux magnitude itself is not treated as voltage and the windings have no conducting connection.

inventory.label: Three-Phase Induction Motor
inventory.definition: Phase-shifted stator currents create a rotating magnetic field that induces rotor currents and torque through relative motion.
inventory.motionThesis: Three stator phases create a constant-magnitude rotating field that outruns a conducting cage, while each moving bar’s induced current follows its angle relative to the field.
inventory.distinction: A two-pole resistance-dominated steady-state schematic uses twenty percent slip, five field turns and four cage turns per cycle; the rotor is neither permanently magnetized nor synchronized to the field.

inventory.label: Generator Synchronization
inventory.definition: Generator synchronization matches an incoming generator’s voltage magnitude, frequency, and phase to a live bus before its connecting breaker closes.
inventory.motionThesis: An incoming voltage vector converges on the live-bus vector, and a physically drawn breaker closes only after their magnitude, phase, and frequency match.
inventory.distinction: A single-phase equivalent assumes the same phase sequence; connection continuity after synchronization does not imply a particular real-power load or replace full three-phase synchronism checks.

inventory.label: Grid Frequency Response
inventory.definition: A power imbalance changes synchronous-grid frequency while stored rotor energy and governor action limit the departure.
inventory.motionThesis: A new electrical load connects, the coupled turbine-generator slows, and delayed mechanical input produces a frequency nadir followed by partial recovery.
inventory.distinction: An illustrative swing-equation and first-order governor response retains primary-control frequency offset and frequency-sensitive load relief; secondary restoration is not implied.

inventory.label: Regenerative Braking
inventory.definition: Regenerative braking operates a traction machine as a generator to transfer vehicle kinetic energy into electrical storage.
inventory.motionThesis: A car decelerates with correctly rolling wheels while opposing generator torque transfers part of the lost kinetic energy into a battery.
inventory.distinction: Wheel angle follows distance, battery charge follows lost squared speed, and a separate heat route accounts for an illustrative twenty percent loss rather than claiming a product efficiency.

inventory.label: Reversible Heat Pump
inventory.definition: A reversible vapor-compression heat pump uses a reversing valve to swap the indoor and outdoor coils’ heating and cooling roles.
inventory.motionThesis: A four-port valve reconnects the refrigerant circuit so the indoor coil changes from heat delivery to heat absorption while compressor flow keeps the same direction.
inventory.distinction: Explicit valve passages and a bidirectional expansion device show circuit reversal; crossed valve passages remain isolated and heat transfer includes absorbed environmental heat as well as compressor work.

inventory.label: Compressed-Air Energy Storage
inventory.definition: Compressed-air energy storage compresses air into a reservoir and later expands the stored air through a generator.
inventory.motionThesis: A shrinking compressor gas space delivers air into a rigid reservoir, then a separate expander releases the stored mass and generates electricity.
inventory.distinction: An ideal isothermal mass balance links piston volume, pressure and valve thresholds; visible heat exchange distinguishes the schematic from real diabatic or adiabatic storage designs.

inventory.label: Point-Absorber Wave Generator
inventory.definition: A point-absorber wave generator extracts energy from a buoy’s vertical motion relative to a reaction structure.
inventory.motionThesis: A buoy heaves out of phase with the water surface, driving a fixed linear generator whose resisting force opposes velocity and whose power peaks between stroke endpoints.
inventory.distinction: An illustrative damped harmonic response keeps buoy displacement distinct from wave elevation and extracts power on both stroke directions without claiming one-way electrical current.

inventory.label: Binary Geothermal Power
inventory.definition: Binary geothermal power transfers heat from geothermal water to a separate low-boiling working fluid that drives a closed-cycle turbine.
inventory.motionThesis: Liquid geothermal water heats an isolated secondary fluid, which vaporizes, expands through a turbine, condenses and is pumped back to the heat exchanger.
inventory.distinction: Separate heater channels keep geothermal water out of the turbine; heat rejection and pump demand accompany net electrical output in an illustrative steady-flow Rankine cycle.

inventory.label: Molten-Salt Thermal Storage
inventory.definition: Molten-salt thermal storage retains useful heat in hot liquid salt and later supplies it to a power block.
inventory.motionThesis: Sunlight transfers a conserved salt inventory from a cold tank through a receiver into a hot tank, then electricity continues after sunset as the hot salt returns through a heat exchanger.
inventory.distinction: Equal-height tanks store sensible heat rather than gravitational head; both salt states stay liquid and separate charging and discharge circuits follow the changing tank inventories.

inventory.label: Thermohaline Overturning
inventory.definition: Thermohaline overturning is large-scale ocean circulation associated with seawater-density differences caused by temperature and salinity.
inventory.motionThesis: Surface parcels cool and receive rejected salt beneath polar ice, sink into a cold deep return, then warm and freshen through a broad mixing return.
inventory.distinction: A schematic overturning cell combines density formation with mixing and upwelling; it is neither a geographic map nor a claim that the global circulation has a single cause.

inventory.label: Coastal Upwelling
inventory.definition: Coastal upwelling replaces offshore-moving surface water with colder water rising from below.
inventory.motionThesis: Equatorward wind drives offshore surface transport while deep water curves upward along the coast carrying nutrients into a lifted thermocline.
inventory.distinction: A steady Northern Hemisphere west-coast section uses a divergence-free schematic flow; the out-of-page wind is distinct from the leftward surface transport and tracers remain on open water streamlines.

inventory.label: Ekman Spiral
inventory.definition: The classical Ekman spiral describes a wind-driven current that weakens and rotates with depth under friction and Coriolis acceleration.
inventory.motionThesis: Water markers remain at fixed depths while moving in progressively turned and weaker horizontal currents, with a plan-view key showing surface flow and integrated transport to the wind’s right.
inventory.distinction: The Northern Hemisphere constant-eddy-viscosity, deep homogeneous-water model separates the velocity profile from parcel trajectories; the exact infinite-depth transport is not inferred from the seven displayed samples.

inventory.label: Estuarine Salt Wedge
inventory.definition: A salt-wedge estuary holds dense seawater beneath a strongly stratified, seaward-flowing layer of river water.
inventory.motionThesis: A stronger river-flow cue accompanies seaward retreat of a sharply bounded saline wedge, whose water parcels move with its changing volume before returning inland as the flow relaxes.
inventory.distinction: An illustrative quasi-static intrusion law uses an area-preserving saline material map and exchange through the open ocean boundary; it is not a solved hydraulic estuary or a deep-ocean overturning cell.

inventory.label: Turbidity Current
inventory.definition: A turbidity current is a downslope gravity flow made denser than surrounding water by transported sediment.
inventory.motionThesis: A bottom-hugging sediment pulse advances down a submarine slope while coarse grains settle first and finer grains remain suspended farther downstream.
inventory.distinction: An illustrative dilute pulse preserves twelve grains as they change from suspension to stationary deposits; it does not imply that all observed turbidity currents lack dense basal layers.

inventory.label: Rip-Current Circulation
inventory.definition: A rip current is a narrow seaward flow that returns wave-delivered nearshore water through the surf zone, often through a gap in a sandbar.
inventory.motionThesis: Shoreward transport over two bars feeds converging alongshore currents, which accelerate through a central gap and spread into two horizontal return cells.
inventory.distinction: An illustrative divergence-free plan-view field resolves feeders, a seaward jet and outer returns; it represents horizontal circulation rather than a vertical undertow or a radiation-stress calculation.

inventory.label: Longshore Sediment Transport
inventory.definition: Longshore sediment transport is the net movement of coastal sediment along a shoreline under obliquely arriving waves and associated nearshore flow.
inventory.motionThesis: Grains move diagonally up a beach in swash and straight downslope in backwash, leaving growing zigzag histories and a cumulative alongshore displacement.
inventory.distinction: A kinematic beach-drift sequence preserves each grain through three swash/backwash cycles; it shows sediment movement along the shore rather than a rip-current return or a sediment-flux prediction.

inventory.label: Tsunami Shoaling
inventory.definition: Tsunami shoaling is the slowing, wavelength shortening and amplitude increase of a long wave entering shallower water.
inventory.motionThesis: Identifiable crests slow and crowd together across a rising shelf while their amplitude grows with the changing water depth.
inventory.distinction: A linear long-wave and Green-law shelf transformation conserves amplitude-squared times phase speed; surface displacement is visually exaggerated and the field stops before run-up or breaking.

inventory.label: Ocean Internal Wave
inventory.definition: An ocean internal wave propagates along a density boundary inside stratified water.
inventory.motionThesis: A travelling density interface passes through nearly stationary water while tracers above and below execute oppositely directed horizontal oscillations.
inventory.distinction: A small-amplitude two-layer rigid-lid mode uses linear velocity potentials; no surface storm or parcel riding along the crest is implied.

inventory.label: Groundwater Cone of Depression
inventory.definition: Pumping lowers groundwater head around a well, forming a cone-shaped drawdown surface.
inventory.motionThesis: A screened well extracts water as the surrounding water table falls most strongly near the pump and a nearby observation well follows the local head.
inventory.distinction: This is an illustrative unconfined cross-section with a prescribed drawdown and recovery, not a hollow underground bowl or a calibrated pumping test.

inventory.label: Artesian Aquifer
inventory.definition: An artesian aquifer is a confined permeable layer whose pressure raises water in a penetrating well above the aquifer top.
inventory.motionThesis: Recharge on high ground drives confined seepage downslope while water rises in a standpipe to a marked pressure head below its rim.
inventory.distinction: The nonflowing artesian example distinguishes pressure head from aquifer elevation; porous layers are not open subterranean rivers.

inventory.label: Meander Cutoff
inventory.definition: A meander cutoff creates a shorter river route across a bend and can isolate the abandoned loop as an oxbow lake.
inventory.motionThesis: A narrow neck opens into a shortcut before sediment plugs disconnect the old loop, leaving an oxbow beside the through-flowing river.
inventory.distinction: A staged plan-view neck cutoff separates channel connection, flow diversion and deposition; erosion and geological time are compressed.

inventory.label: Watershed Divide
inventory.definition: A watershed divide is a topographic boundary separating surface runoff that drains to different outlets.
inventory.motionThesis: Rain lands on opposite flanks of a central ridge and follows branching channels into two separate outlet streams.
inventory.distinction: The divide is fixed topography; the schematic follows surface drainage and does not assert an identical groundwater divide.

inventory.label: Impervious Runoff
inventory.definition: Impervious surfaces reduce infiltration and commonly increase rapid surface runoff during rainfall.
inventory.motionThesis: Equal rain inputs reach two slopes: five of eight water tokens enter soil on the pervious side, while seven of eight reach the paved-side surface outlet.
inventory.distinction: Eight equal-volume tokens per side illustrate a chosen budget, not field-calibrated runoff fractions; retained subsurface water remains visible after the storm.

inventory.label: Ice-Albedo Feedback
inventory.definition: Loss of reflective ice can increase absorbed sunlight and promote further warming and ice loss.
inventory.motionThesis: The same incoming solar rays meet a retreating ice edge: more rays terminate as heat in dark water and fewer return upward as reflection.
inventory.distinction: Six equal incoming energy packets use illustrative ice and water reflection choices; a staged forced retreat explains positive feedback without a climate-rate prediction.

inventory.label: Ice-Shelf Buttressing
inventory.definition: A floating ice shelf can restrain grounded ice flow through lateral contact and other resistive stresses.
inventory.motionThesis: A confined shelf loses its margin-contacting front section; upstream ice markers then advance faster past the grounding line into the remaining shelf.
inventory.distinction: A plan-view pinned-shelf example shows removal of lateral restraint, not direct sea-level rise from melting floating ice or a universal response of every shelf.

inventory.label: Thermokarst Thaw Slump
inventory.definition: Melting ground ice can undermine an ice-rich slope and cause a retreating thaw headwall and downslope sediment movement.
inventory.motionThesis: Three turf blocks lose support after their underlying ice lenses thin, then descend onto a muddy apron as the exposed headwall retreats upslope.
inventory.distinction: A finite thaw episode tracks the same soil blocks and exported meltwater; this differs from a dry landslide and does not conserve soil volume by replacing melted ice.

inventory.label: El Nino-Southern Oscillation
inventory.definition: ENSO is coupled tropical Pacific variability involving trade winds, ocean temperatures and atmospheric convection.
inventory.motionThesis: Westward trades weaken before the eastern thermocline deepens, warm water expands eastward and convection shifts from the western Pacific.
inventory.distinction: This normal-to-warm-phase explanatory transition exaggerates subsurface depth changes; its repeating presentation is not an ENSO forecast or a regular climate clock.

inventory.label: Atmospheric River
inventory.definition: An atmospheric river is a long narrow corridor of concentrated water-vapor transport.
inventory.motionThesis: A coherent moisture corridor crosses the ocean toward a coastline, where landfall and coastal mountains concentrate precipitation.
inventory.distinction: An illustrative map separates horizontal vapor transport from landfall rain; the corridor is gaseous moisture, not a liquid channel or a complete storm forecast.

inventory.label: Orographic Rain Shadow
inventory.definition: A mountain can promote precipitation on its windward side while descending air warms and dries on its lee side.
inventory.motionThesis: One moist air parcel rises and expands over a mountain, forms cloud and loses water as rain, then descends smaller and clearer on the lee side.
inventory.distinction: The parcel radius varies schematically with elevation, and cloud opacity follows condensation then evaporation; lee air retains vapor and need not be universally rainless.

inventory.label: Frost Heave by Ice-Lens Growth
inventory.definition: Frost heave can result when migrating groundwater freezes into subsurface ice lenses that lift overlying soil.
inventory.motionThesis: Water rises through pores into a growing ice lens while the supported turf layer lifts by the added lens thickness and the lower water store falls.
inventory.distinction: The illustrative frost-susceptible soil is fed by external water migration; heave is not attributed merely to local water expanding on freezing.

inventory.label: Seismic Base Isolation
inventory.definition: Seismic isolation bearings lengthen a structure's vibration period and accommodate movement between its foundation and superstructure.
inventory.motionThesis: A shaking foundation shears laminated bearings while the rigid building above moves much less in a consistent steady harmonic response.
inventory.distinction: The chosen forcing frequency is three times the isolated natural frequency; shear geometry follows connected bearing endpoints and does not imply isolation at every frequency.

inventory.label: Tuned Mass Damper
inventory.definition: A secondary oscillator can reduce a structure's response near a selected excitation frequency by exchanging energy and dissipating relative motion.
inventory.motionThesis: A guided roof mass moves relative to a swaying building through a visible spring and dashpot, following the coupled two-mass harmonic solution.
inventory.distinction: The primary and absorber use mass ratio 0.1 and tuned stiffness under a single-frequency drive; the relative motion is solved rather than assumed to be exactly opposite.

inventory.label: Prestressed Concrete
inventory.definition: Prestressing introduces deliberate compression into concrete before service loading.
inventory.motionThesis: A jack tensions an eccentric tendon, anchors retain it after the jack retracts, and the later service load partly cancels the beam's upward camber.
inventory.distinction: This post-tensioning sequence uses illustrative elastic camber and retained prestress; it is not a design calculation or a claim that all concrete remains uncracked at every load.

inventory.label: Truss Load Paths
inventory.definition: A pin-jointed truss carries joint loads through axial tension and compression in connected triangular members.
inventory.motionThesis: Loads transfer between two upper joints while signed member-force colors and widths change with exact joint equilibrium.
inventory.distinction: The determinate five-joint truss assumes pin joints, axial members and loads applied only at joints; deformation is omitted rather than invented.

inventory.label: Arch Thrust
inventory.definition: An arch transfers loads to its abutments with horizontal as well as vertical reactions.
inventory.motionThesis: A load traverses a three-hinged arch while springing reactions change, including opposed horizontal thrust at the abutments.
inventory.distinction: For span L and rise f the crown-hinge equation gives H=P min(a,L-a)/(2f); point loading does not make this parabolic arch a pure-compression funicular.

inventory.label: Cantilever Deflection
inventory.definition: A clamped elastic beam curves under load while its root remains fixed in position and slope.
inventory.motionThesis: An increasing end load bends a constant-thickness cantilever with maximum movement at its free tip and a fixed horizontal root.
inventory.distinction: The small-deflection Euler-Bernoulli shape w=delta xiÂ²(3-xi)/2 is used; displayed displacement is exaggerated and is not an exact large-rotation beam solution.

inventory.label: Cable-Stayed Load Transfer
inventory.definition: Cable stays support deck loads in tension and transfer their vertical components into a compression tower.
inventory.motionThesis: Paired deck loads move between stay anchors while the loaded stays brighten and thicken, transferring balanced forces into a fixed tower.
inventory.distinction: An ideal symmetric pin-panel model shares each moving load between adjacent anchors with positive dead load; stays never carry compression and horizontal tower forces balance.

inventory.label: Bridge Expansion Joint
inventory.definition: A bridge expansion joint accommodates deck movement while maintaining a traffic-supporting connection.
inventory.motionThesis: Warming deck ends translate toward each other and their alternating steel fingers interleave more deeply without colliding.
inventory.distinction: The exaggerated thermal motion reduces root gap from 24 to 16 units; 14-unit fingers retain at least two units of clearance from the opposing root.

inventory.label: Tunnel-Boring Advance
inventory.definition: A tunnel-boring machine excavates while reacting thrust against installed lining, then installs the next lining ring.
inventory.motionThesis: The cutter and shield advance one ring length against the completed lining; advance pauses while a new ring is assembled behind the shield and the jacks regrip.
inventory.distinction: A side cutaway compresses one excavation-and-lining cycle; ring installation occurs behind the shield, and spoil travels back toward the finished tunnel.

inventory.label: Clarifier Sedimentation
inventory.definition: A clarifier separates settleable suspended solids from water using gravity and removes collected sludge.
inventory.motionThesis: Coarse solids descend through a baffled tank while one fine tracer reaches the overflow; a floor scraper collects settled solids into the hopper.
inventory.distinction: A finite rectangular-tank episode uses prescribed settling velocities and a separate scraper pass; the fine escaping fraction prevents a claim of complete removal.

inventory.label: Activated-Sludge Treatment
inventory.definition: Activated sludge uses aerated microbial flocs to consume organic matter, followed by settling and biomass return.
inventory.motionThesis: Organic feed joins aerated flocs, then flocs settle in a second tank; most follow a return pipe to the reactor while one leaves through a waste branch.
inventory.distinction: The process schematic emphasizes biological uptake and retained floc identity through recycle; bubble motion alone is not the cleaning mechanism and no quantitative carbon balance is claimed.

inventory.label: Roundabout Gap Acceptance
inventory.definition: A roundabout entrant yields until a suitable gap in circulating traffic permits entry.
inventory.motionThesis: An approaching car waits through a short gap, enters tangentially during a longer one and joins counterclockwise traffic before leaving at an exit.
inventory.distinction: A scripted slow-speed example demonstrates rejected and accepted headways, not a universal critical gap or a calibrated traffic-capacity model.

inventory.label: Zipper Merge
inventory.definition: A zipper merge alternates vehicles from two congested approach lanes into one lane at a closure.
inventory.motionThesis: Two queues advance to a taper and release one vehicle from each lane in alternating reserved slots into the shared downstream lane.
inventory.distinction: The example assumes slow congested traffic with slot-based admission; it does not prescribe late merging at arbitrary highway speeds.

inventory.label: Traffic Shock Wave
inventory.definition: A traffic shock wave is a moving boundary between different traffic-flow states.
inventory.motionThesis: Cars continue forward while their braking boundary travels backward; each car slows only when it reaches that boundary.
inventory.distinction: The piecewise states k1=.04,v1=10 and k2=.1,v2=2 give shock speed -10/3 by vehicle conservation; road length and the finite episode are schematic.

inventory.label: Railway Track Circuit
inventory.definition: A track circuit detects rail occupancy when conductive wheels and axles shunt current away from a relay.
inventory.motionThesis: A train's axles bridge the rails, the relay drops and the signal turns restrictive until the final axle clears the insulated section.
inventory.distinction: The simplified DC circuit shows occupancy shunting and de-energization, not every possible railway signaling failure or a complete operational interlocking.

inventory.label: Ship-to-Shore Container Crane
inventory.definition: A ship-to-shore crane transfers containers between a vessel and quayside transport using a travelling trolley and hoist.
inventory.motionThesis: A spreader locks onto a shipboard container, raises it clear of the stack, traverses to the quay, lowers it onto a chassis and returns empty.
inventory.distinction: One container retains its identity through lock, lift, traverse, touchdown and release; cycle time and port geometry are compressed.

inventory.label: Rocket Stage Separation
inventory.definition: Rocket staging releases spent propulsion hardware so a continuing vehicle no longer carries its mass.
inventory.motionThesis: After engine cutoff and a short coast, a visible joint opens and the spent stage recedes before the upper engine ignites.
inventory.distinction: A cold-staging example uses a frame moving with the upper vehicle; receding hardware is not shown falling in a ground-fixed frame and the sequence is not universal to hot staging.

inventory.label: Reaction-Wheel Attitude Control
inventory.definition: A reaction wheel exchanges angular momentum with its spacecraft to change attitude without expelling propellant.
inventory.motionThesis: An internal wheel turns relative to the spacecraft while the bus rotates in the opposite direction, then both reverse smoothly to close the demonstration.
